items.label: text
items.text: Make a solution of your suspected sulfate in distilled (pure) water, add some dilute hydrochloric acid and then add some barium chloride solution. A sulfate will produce a white precipitate of barium sulfate.

items.label: formula
items.text: B a ^ { 2 + ( a q ) } + S O _ { 4 } { ^ { 2 - ( a q ) } } \rightarrow B a S O _ { 4 } ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: You add acid to the solution to react with and remove other anions which might also produce white precipitates when you add the barium chloride solution. For example, if you didn't add acid, you would also obtain a white precipitate if there were carbonate ions present. This is because barium carbonate is also white and insoluble. The acid reacts with the carbonate ions and removes them. It is important to remember that the acid must be added before the barium chloride solution.

items.label: text
items.text: You must never acidify the solution with sulfuric acid because sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions. If you add those, you are bound to get a precipitate of barium sulfate because you have added sulfate ions.

items.label: text
items.text: Make a solution of your suspected chloride, bromide or iodide and add enough dilute nitric acid to make it acidic. Then add some silver nitrate solution.

items.label: text
items.text: A white precipitate (of silver chloride) shows the presence of chloride ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: A g ^ { + } ( a q ) + C I ^ { - } ( a q ) \rightarrow A g C I ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: A cream precipitate (of silver bromide) shows the presence of bromide ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: A g ^ { + } ( a q ) + B r ^ { - } ( a q ) \rightarrow A g B r ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: A yellow precipitate (of silver iodide) shows the presence of iodide ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: A g ^ { + } ( a q ) + 1 - ( a q ) \to A g | ( s )
